messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Marcus

Marcus Volkov, forty-nine, sits in the leather chair across from the therapist with his shoulders drawn inward, his hands folded tightly in his lap. He is a city council member in a mid-sized Midwestern city—the kind of position that demands visibility, composure, a steady hand at community meetings and ribbon cuttings. For the past eighteen months, he has been drowning.

It began on a patrol in Kandahar in 2009. Marcus was a captain then, leading a convoy through a market district. The intelligence had been solid—or so they'd been told. He remembers the weight of the body armor, the dust in his throat, the way the market had gone quiet all at once. Then the IED detonated beneath the second Humvee. He remembers screaming, the smell, the shape of something that might have been a leg. But when he tries to reconstruct the sequence—who was where, what he did in the first seconds, whether he called for the medic or whether someone else did—the memory fractures. Whole stretches are simply gone, replaced by a kind of white noise. Three soldiers died. He knows this. He knows he was there. But the specifics slip away like water through his hands, and when he tries to speak about it, even to himself in the privacy of his home, the words dissolve mid-sentence and he is left gasping, the terror of that moment flooding back into his chest as though it were happening now.

The terror is the worst part. When he forces himself to remember—when he sits alone and tries to piece together what happened—his body responds as if the threat is immediate and real. His heart races. His breathing becomes shallow. His muscles tense as though preparing to dive for cover. Marcus had come to believe that his body was working against him, that it was fundamentally broken, still wired for a danger that no longer existed. He was certain the world remained as lethal as it had been in that market, that safety was an illusion people told themselves. The hypervigilance was constant. He had to be watching, always, for the signs that something was about to go wrong. His wife, Elena, had stopped trying to touch him months ago. When she reached for his arm during dinner or placed a hand on his shoulder in the kitchen, he would flinch violently, his entire body recoiling as though from a live wire. The look on her face each time—a mixture of hurt and resignation—had become another thing he couldn't bear to remember.

To manage the intrusions, Marcus had developed a system. The moment a memory threatened to surface, or when his thoughts began spiraling into catastrophic loops about what might happen if he let his guard down, he would turn on the television or blast music through the speakers in his home office. The noise was a wall. It kept the fragments at bay, filled the spaces where the memories might take hold. At first it had worked—the distraction bought him hours of relative peace. But over time, the strategy had begun to backfire. The sensory flooding seemed to intensify his sense that he couldn't trust anything, that even in his own home he needed external noise to keep himself from dissolving. The constant monitoring of his own thoughts—the exhausting surveillance of his own mind for signs of breakdown—had become its own form of torture. He would catch himself spiraling and then begin monitoring that spiral, watching himself for evidence of losing control, which only deepened his conviction that his mind, like his body, was no longer reliable. When the noise stopped, when he was forced into silence, the fragmented images would rush back with even more force, and his appraisals about the world's danger would crystallize into certainty.

The sleep had gone first. He would lie awake until two or three in the morning, unable to shut off the vigilance, unable to trust that the house was secure even though he had checked the locks four times. Elena had moved to the guest room six months ago. At city council meetings, he found himself struggling to concentrate, his mind half-listening to constituents while the other half monitored the room for exits, for threats, for the moment when everything would fall apart. Two weeks ago, during a public forum about zoning regulations, he had blanked mid-sentence, unable to find his way back to what he had been saying. The silence had stretched. People had stared. He had excused himself and driven home, where he sat in the dark with the television blaring, unable to move.

It was Elena who finally insisted he seek help. She had found him that evening, still in his coat, still in the dark, and she had said something that cut through the noise: "I can't reach you anymore." Marcus knows she is right. He is terrified that if he stops the distraction, stops the monitoring, stops the avoidance, the memories will consume him entirely. But he is also beginning to understand that the very things he has done to survive are now the things that are destroying his life.
